THE CHINA MAIL
一
MAY RETIRE?
Mukden, March 15.

Marshall Chang Tso-lin has wired to the Chief Executive, Marshall Tuan, stating that in conformity with the law of Nature and with the trend of popular will, he had advanced his troops into Chilli beyond the Great Wall with a view to expellings, those "wicked" officials, who are taking exclusive possession of political power in Pelding, as well as to maintaining peace and order in North China.

Marshall Chang Two-lin to-day held a meeting with the Chairman of the local Chinese Chamber of Commerce and representatives of various public bodies, with whom he exchanged views respecting measures to save the situation and also questions of financial consolidation and of the appointment of a Civil Governor of Fengtian. It is observed that Marshall Chang has finally decided to settle the questions in accordance with the popular will and that in view of the situation he will refrain from his coming Birthday celebrations.
If a further added that upon the restoration of normal condition, he intended to give up his military power, to go into retirement, and to share the smiles and frown of fortune with the populhee.
It is understood that he will shortly proceed to Kaoshantzu in order to lead a quiet life for a while.—Eastern News Agency.

ASKIEID BY THE PEKING
CABINEP.
(Reuter's Service.)

It is officially announced this afternoon that the Cuisined this morning decided to adopt a proposal preferred by the Minister of Finance for the rotation of a new internal loan of $20,000,000 which will be known as the fifteenth year loan of the Republic.
Peking, Manch 16.

It will be secured on the German Boxer Indemnity funds. Interest will be at eight per cent. and the loan will be floated at ninety, after which six per cent. will be deducted by the bankers for commission. It will be taken up in three monthly instruments.

The purposes for which the proceeds will be expended are officially stated as follows: (b) to redeem the Spring Festival Treasury Bonds recently issued to the amount of eight "million dollars; (2) to meet the expenses of Chinese legations and consulates abroad for a period of three years, and (3) to meet the administrative and military expenses of the Central Government for the same period.

Dr. Reginald M. Atwater, instructor in epidemiology at the Harvard Medical School who has just returned from a visit to the Far East, discussing the obstacles to public health progress in China, at Boston on February 15, said: "Heraps the most significant of a life in inertia that comes from the firm adherence to traditions which have been their heritage through these thousands of years. The dependence of the masses on wrong ideas of disease, veneration of the old because it is old rather than because it is good, general distrust of the new because it is new, failure to profit by the scientific method and a fatal tendency to laissez-faire, these are the real obstacles to public health."

CHARLES FORBES.
The United States Supreme Court has denied a review of the conviction of Charles Forbes, former director of the Veterans Bureau, Forbes must serve two years in the Federal prison.—"China Press."

STRIKE FEVER.

Subsequent to the suspension for three days of one of the ring-leaders at the Nagul Wata Kalsha Mill No. 4, Shanghai who incited the workers to insist on holiday to observe the anniversary of Dr. Sun's death, the workers raised a rumpus and made trouble. The riot became so bad that the police were called in from Pootoo Road station, states the Chinese press, who tried to beat back the mob with rattan sticks. Continuing, the journal aserts that a foreign police officer fired a shot into the air. Intimidate those concerned. Although this has been denied in the channel, says the: "N.C. Daily News," the workers demand that in future police shall be forbidden entrance into the mill premises. At any rate the mob left without inflicting serious damage to one tittings.
The labourers have presented the following demands to the management:

1. The xingleader must be ex-
cused unconutionally.

2. Full pay for the past three days, during the strike.
3. The management to pay $50 to each of six so-called injured workers.
4. The police are to be prohibited from entering the mills and displaying or using five arms.
Although the strike is not of such magnitude to cause much alarm is nevertheless an incident which serves to keep alive the unrest among the industrials.

The Postal strike, which was expected for March 16, says the same paper, did not take place after an all-night meeting between Mr. V. Stapleton Cotton, the Acting Postal Commissioner, Mr. Zing, the Deputy Postal Commissioner, and the representatives of the workers. A compromise on the "workers' demands was reached, which, in effect, means little, more than that they agree to wait for a full discussion of their demands with Mr. Tolfelsen, the permanent Commissioner in Shanghai, when he returns from Home early next month.
The demands and the tactics of the workers seem to indicate that there was nothing to strike about, that, in former days they would have petitioned for the slight changes they desire, which, in due course, would have been granted. The questions over which the workers have become agitated are apparently entirely administrative, and involve the growth of the city and the necessity for reorganisation to handle the greater volume of mail matter which comes to Shanghai from all parts of the world. If the questions are left to the Postal authorities and their own employees there can be little question but that Mr. Tollefsen will find a solution, but the danger here, as in the textile industry, lies in outside influences which seize upon the slightest grievance and turn it into a great industrial problem.

REPORT ON THE IMPERIAL COLLEGE.
SELECTION FOR ADMISSION.
The Principal's Report of the Imperial College of Imperial Agriculture Trinidad Co., copy of which has been received from the Colonial Secretary's Office, says, inter aliv:—

The Academic Year 1924-25 constitutes the third in the life of the College, and with its first students to complete the Diploma Course have passed into the world.
I arrived in Trinidad on August 23, 1924, so that the year under review covers almost exactly my first year of occupancy of the post of Principal Sir Francis Watta, K.G.M.G., my predecessor, took leave preparatory to retirement on July 1, 1924, and retired on October 31, 1924. The College is the readmission of schemes which he had long carried in his mind, and which he, happier than many another, was enabled to see reach their fruition during his active career. This is not the place to give a record of his services. As first Principal of the College he served it for two years, and we wish him well in his retirement.

There has been no increase of the staff, and only one change in the personnel. Professor W. W. Dunlop resigned on September 30, and Mr. C. Y. Shepard, E.S.C. (Econ.), joined the staff as Lecturer in Economics, to be subsequently promoted to the post of Professor of Economics on July 10, 1925.

The Entrance Examination, which had hitherto been held for the admission to the Diploma Course of those students who did not possess any accepted qualification, having proved unworkable in practice, was discontinued, and replaced by a system of recommendation. During the course of the year the methods of selection for admission have been further explored, and the results incorporated in the prospectus for 1926-27. The matters is not a simple one, in view of the Imperial nature of the College and the fact that students may come from all over the globe. Already we have students admitted on Canadian and South African qualifications, while enquiries have been received from India, Malaysia and Australia.

Admissions to the Diploma Course for the Session 1924-25 were six, making a total in the College of 18. In addition, 12 students of whom six were sent by the Empire Cotton Growing Corporation and four by the Colonial Office joined the College to take a post-graduate course, while four joined to take a special one-year course.
The final Diploma examination was held in June, 1925, which seven students appeared and five qualified for the Diploma. Of these one has secured employment in Barbados, one in Guadeloupe, while two have returned to take a fourth year course.
Of the leaving, post-graduate students, four have taken appointments in the Gold Coast, two in South Africa, and one in Ceylon. One is joining the recently established Cotton Research Station in Trinidad, and two are employed on Trinidad estates. Of the special students, two remain on at the College to take a further course, while one has secured employment in a local sugar factory. The total number of students in residence was, therefore, 34.
Dueling the year the conditions for the Associateship have been laid down, and the first Associateship has been awarded to Mr. J. C. Hopkins. Post-graduate students who have already left are now eligible for the Associateship.

In view of the strength of the staff, which has to meet the needs of a three-year Diploma course as well as advanced course for past graduates, the amount of research carried out is necessarily limited. In regard to bananas, the report states:

In regard to sugar the report states: — An investigation, limited by the area available, on seeding canes, especially with regard to milling capacity, has been undertaken. The main investigation, however, concerns the froghopper's pest of the canes in Trinidad. A considerable amount of detailed work on this subject is being carried out by the entomological section. This work aims at tracing the relationship between host and parasite, especially with a view to determining the causes of differential susceptibility. A suggestive paper on the subject, written by Dr. Withycombe, is now in the press.

An informal committee has been established from the combined staffs of the Department of Agriculture and the College to study the entire problem of banana cultivation and the trade. The prime consideration is the production of a banana immune to Panama disease and at the same time acceptable to the trade. Trial shipments have been made with the Giant Fig, and efforts have been made to quase bananas from seedlings. Before the end of the year under report Dr. Harland, with the same object in view and through the kind financial assistance of the Imperial Research Committee, started upon a tour to the Eastern hemisphere to study the banana. A cytological investigation has been undertaken which has shown a varietal difference in the chromosome number.
NUPTIALS

A pretty wedding took place at Christ Church, Ealing, on February 8, when members of two old Ealing families were united. The bridegroom was Mr. Albert Edward Sayers, third son of Mr. and Mrs. A. V. Sayers, Spring Bridge-road, Ealing, and the bride Miss Margaret Ivy Kondall, daughter of the late Inspector Kendall, of Hongkong, and of Mrs. Sayers, 3, Uxbridge Road, Ealing.

The bride, who was dressed in a fuchsin dross with hat to tone, was given away by her stepfather, Mr. A. E. Sayers. She was attended by her sister, who was attired in a golden brown velvet dress, with hat to match. The best man was Mr. Leslie Sayers, brother of the bridedroom.

After the ceremony, a reception was held at 3 Uxbridge-road.
The happy couple were the recipients of suitable gifts from the bridegroom's parents and the bride's mother. Others who gave presents were Miss W. Kendall, Mr. F. Kendall, Mr. A. El. Sayers and Messrs. W. and A. Sayers, Mrs. Currival and Miss Eager, Mr. and Mrs. Feakes, Mr. H. Feakes, Mrs. Harris, Mr. and Mrs. H.
